messages.content: What is technical analysis and what are its core assumptions?

Technical analysis (TA): Studying price charts and volume to forecast future price movements. Core assumptions: 1. Market discounts everything — price reflects all known information. 2. Prices move in trends — trending is persistent until disruption. 3. History repeats — patterns recur because human psychology is consistent. Key tools: Chart patterns, trend lines, support/resistance, moving averages, oscillators, volume analysis. TA vs. fundamental analysis: FA focuses on intrinsic value; TA focuses on price behaviour. TA more useful for timing entry/exit; FA for stock selection. Criticisms: Subjective pattern recognition, self-fulfilling prophecy, random walk hypothesis. Most professional traders use both: FA to select what to trade, TA to determine when.
Explain support and resistance levels.

Support: Price level where buying interest historically prevents further decline. Acts as a floor. Resistance: Price level where selling pressure historically prevents further advance. Acts as a ceiling. Key principle — role reversal: Once broken, support becomes resistance and vice versa. Why they work: Psychological anchoring — traders remember round numbers and prior highs/lows. Unfilled orders accumulate at key levels. Strength factors: More touches = stronger level. Higher volume at level = stronger. Longer time frame = more significant. Types: Horizontal S/R (prior highs/lows), dynamic S/R (moving averages, trend lines), psychological (round numbers: $100, $1,000). Trading application: Buy near support, sell near resistance. Enter on confirmed break with volume. Set stop just below support (long) or above resistance (short).
What is a moving average and how is it used in trading?

Moving average (MA): Average closing price over N periods — smooths price to reveal trend direction. Simple MA (SMA): Equal weight to all periods. 200-day SMA = long-term trend. 50-day SMA = medium-term trend. 20-day SMA = short-term trend. Exponential MA (EMA): More weight on recent prices — faster reaction. Signals: Price above MA → uptrend. Price below MA → downtrend. MA crossover: 50-day crosses above 200-day = Golden Cross (bullish). 50-day crosses below 200-day = Death Cross (bearish). MA as dynamic support/resistance: Price often pulls back to MA in trending markets. Limitations: Lagging indicator — confirms trend, doesn't predict it. Whipsaws in sideways markets. Use with momentum indicators to filter false signals.
What is RSI and how do traders use it?

RSI (Relative Strength Index): Momentum oscillator measuring speed and magnitude of price changes. Range: 0–100. Formula: RSI = 100 − (100 / (1 + RS)), where RS = average gain / average loss over 14 periods. Overbought: RSI > 70 → potential reversal or pause. Oversold: RSI < 30 → potential bounce or reversal. Trend trading adjustment: In strong uptrend, RSI stays 40–80. In downtrend, RSI stays 20–60. Divergence (most powerful signal): Bullish divergence: Price makes lower low, RSI makes higher low → momentum improving → potential reversal up. Bearish divergence: Price makes higher high, RSI makes lower high → momentum weakening → potential reversal down. RSI alone not sufficient — combine with trend, support/resistance, volume for higher probability trades.
Explain MACD and how it signals buy/sell opportunities.

MACD (Moving Average Convergence Divergence): Trend-following momentum indicator. Components: MACD line = 12-period EMA − 26-period EMA. Signal line = 9-period EMA of MACD line. Histogram = MACD line − signal line. Signals: Crossover: MACD crosses above signal line → bullish. MACD crosses below signal line → bearish. Zero line cross: MACD crosses above 0 → trend turned bullish. MACD crosses below 0 → trend turned bearish. Histogram: Bars growing → momentum building. Bars shrinking → momentum weakening. Divergence: Price trend diverges from MACD → potential reversal. Best used in trending markets — generates many false signals in choppy conditions. Combine with RSI and volume for confirmation. Standard settings (12,26,9) can be adjusted for faster/slower signals.
What is a trend line and how do you draw one correctly?

Trend line: Straight line connecting a series of highs or lows to identify trend direction. Uptrend line: Connect two or more higher lows. Upward sloping. Acts as support — buy on touch. Downtrend line: Connect two or more lower highs. Downward sloping. Acts as resistance — sell on touch. Rules for valid trend line: Minimum two points to draw, three points to confirm. Don't force lines — connect actual price pivots, not body midpoints. Steeper trend lines are less sustainable (>45° breaks more often). Trend line break: Close below uptrend line = potential trend change. Requires confirmation — volume spike, follow-through. Channel: Two parallel trend lines containing price (upper resistance, lower support). Trading channel: Buy lower line, sell upper line, or trade breakout. Trend lines are subjective — different traders draw differently. Use higher time frames for more reliable lines.
What is volume and why is it important in trading?

Volume: Number of shares (or contracts) traded in a period. Most important confirmation tool in technical analysis. Principles: Volume confirms price moves — high volume breakout = strong conviction. Low volume breakout = weak, likely to fail. Volume precedes price — unusual volume often signals coming move. Buying vs. selling volume: Price up + high volume = strong buying. Price up + low volume = weak rally (bearish divergence). Price down + high volume = strong selling. Price down + low volume = weak selling (bullish divergence). Volume indicators: OBV (On-Balance Volume): Cumulative volume — add on up days, subtract on down days. OBV divergence is powerful signal. Volume profile: Shows volume at each price level — high-volume nodes = strong S/R. VWAP (Volume-Weighted Average Price): Institutional benchmark — price trades above/below VWAP matters for institutions.
Explain the head and shoulders pattern.

Head and shoulders (H&S): Reversal pattern signalling trend change from bullish to bearish. Formation: Left shoulder: Rally, partial pullback. Head: Higher rally, deeper pullback. Right shoulder: Rally that fails to reach head's high, then declines. Neckline: Line connecting lows of the two pullbacks. Signal: Break below neckline with volume = confirmed sell signal. Target: Neckline − (Head height − Neckline). Example: Neckline at $50, head at $70 → target = $50 − $20 = $30. Inverse H&S: Same pattern upside down = bullish reversal. Right shoulder volume: Should be lower than left shoulder on H&S top — declining enthusiasm. Neckline slope: Upward-sloping neckline = stronger signal on break. Failure rate: H&S fails ~30% of time — always use stop loss above right shoulder.
What is Fibonacci retracement and how do traders use it?

Fibonacci retracement: Uses Fibonacci ratios (23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8%, 78.6%) to identify potential support/resistance during pullbacks. Based on Fibonacci sequence where each number is sum of prior two. Key levels: 38.2% — shallow retracement (strong trend). 50% — common retracement level (not technically Fibonacci but widely watched). 61.8% — golden ratio — strongest retracement level. 78.6% — deep retracement (trend weakening). How to draw: Swing low to swing high (for uptrend). Levels show where pullback may find support. Trading application: Wait for price to pull back to Fibonacci level, then look for reversal signals (candlestick pattern, volume, RSI). Enter at 38.2–61.8% retracement. Stop below 78.6% (or swing low). Target prior high or Fibonacci extension (127.2%, 161.8%). Confluence: Fib level + horizontal S/R + moving average = high-probability entry.
What is momentum trading and how does it work?

Momentum trading: Buying rising assets, selling (or shorting) falling ones — following trend until exhaustion. Core finding: Stocks that outperformed over past 3–12 months tend to continue outperforming over next 3–12 months (Jegadeesh & Titman 1993 — Nobel-recognised research). Strategies: Relative strength: Buy top quartile performers vs. sector/market. Absolute momentum: Buy asset class only when its trend is positive. Indicators used: Rate of change (ROC), RSI, MACD, ADX (trend strength). Entry timing: Enter after pullback in strong uptrend. Use MA alignment (price > 20 > 50 > 200 SMA = strong momentum). Exit: Price breaks key MA, momentum divergence, sector rotation. Risk: Momentum crashes — during market reversals, momentum stocks hit hardest. Position sizing critical — momentum portfolios need hard stops.
What is mean reversion trading?

Mean reversion: Assets that move far from historical average tend to revert back. Mathematical basis: Prices follow mean-reverting processes in range-bound markets. Indicators: Bollinger Bands (2 standard deviations from 20-period MA). RSI extreme readings (<20, >80). Z-score: How many standard deviations from mean. Strategies: Pairs trading: Two correlated stocks diverge — buy underperformer, short outperformer — profit on convergence. Statistical arbitrage: Quantitative version of pairs trading across many securities. Range trading: Buy at support, sell at resistance in defined range. Risk: Mean reversion fails when new trend begins — mean never reverts in breaking stocks. Can hold underwater positions for extended periods (carries gap risk). Works best in: Sideways markets, highly liquid assets, short holding periods. Less effective in: Strong trending markets, individual momentum stocks.
Explain the concept of risk-reward ratio in trading.

Risk-reward ratio (RRR): Compares potential profit to potential loss on a trade. RRR = (Target price − Entry) / (Entry − Stop loss). Example: Entry $50, Stop $47, Target $59. Risk = $3, Reward = $9. RRR = 3:1. Minimum acceptable RRR: 2:1 for most strategies. 1:1 requires 60%+ win rate to be profitable. Why RRR matters: Win rate of 40% with 3:1 RRR = profitable. Win rate of 60% with 1:1 RRR = break even. Expected value = (Win rate × avg profit) − (Loss rate × avg loss). A trader with 40% win rate and 3:1 RRR: EV = (0.4 × 3) − (0.6 × 1) = 0.6 per trade. Always define risk before entry. Never adjust stops wider after entry — stop loss is a pre-commitment device.
What is position sizing and how should traders approach it?

Position sizing: Determining how many shares/contracts to buy based on account size and risk. Fixed percentage risk model: Risk maximum 1–2% of account per trade. Example: $100,000 account, 1% risk = $1,000 max loss per trade. Trade entry $50, stop $47 ($3 risk per share). Position size = $1,000 / $3 = 333 shares. Kelly Criterion: Mathematical formula for optimal position sizing. Kelly % = Win rate − (Loss rate / Win ratio). Often halved (Half-Kelly) to reduce volatility. Volatility-adjusted sizing: Larger positions in low-volatility setups. Position sizing rules: Never risk more than 2% on single trade. Never have more than 6–8% total portfolio at risk. Reduce size after drawdowns. Scale in/out of positions rather than full commitment at once.
What is the difference between swing trading and day trading?

Day trading: All positions closed by end of trading day. No overnight risk. High frequency of trades (5–20+ daily). Requires real-time monitoring. Tools: Level 2 quotes, time & sales, intraday charts (1-min, 5-min, 15-min). Costs: Commissions, bid-ask spread — significant at high frequency. PDT rule (US): Accounts <$25,000 limited to 3 day trades per 5 days. Swing trading: Hold positions days to weeks. Captures larger moves — lower transaction cost relative to gain. Analyse daily/weekly charts. Less time-intensive — suitable for employed traders. Overnight risk: earnings, news events. Position trading: Weeks to months — follows major trends. Fundamental analysis more important. Which to choose: Day trading: capital-intensive, stressful, high skill threshold. Most day traders lose money. Swing trading: More accessible, time-efficient, still requires discipline.
Explain candlestick patterns and their significance.

Candlestick chart: Each candle shows open, high, low, close for a period. Body: Distance between open and close. Wick/shadow: High and low beyond body. Bullish candle (close > open): Often white or green. Bearish candle (close < open): Often black or red. Key single-candle patterns: Doji: Open = close. Indecision. Hammer: Small body, long lower wick — bullish reversal at bottom. Shooting star: Small body, long upper wick — bearish reversal at top. Marubozu: No wicks — strong directional conviction. Two-candle patterns: Bullish engulfing: Green candle fully engulfs prior red — bullish reversal. Bearish engulfing: Red candle fully engulfs prior green — bearish reversal. Three-candle patterns: Morning star: Red, doji, green — bullish reversal. Evening star: Opposite — bearish reversal. Key: Candlestick patterns at key S/R levels have much higher reliability.
What is the Average True Range (ATR) and how is it used?

ATR: Measures market volatility — average of true ranges over N periods (default 14). True range = max of: (High − Low), |High − Prior Close|, |Low − Prior Close|. High ATR: High volatility — wider price swings. Low ATR: Low volatility — price consolidating. Uses: Stop placement: Set stop 1.5–2× ATR below entry to avoid being stopped by normal noise. Position sizing: Reduce position size when ATR high (more volatile = more risk per share). Breakout filter: Volume AND price expansion beyond ATR = genuine breakout. Trend strength: ATR rising during trend = healthy trend. ATR declining = trend losing momentum. ATR-based trailing stop: Update stop to 2× ATR below current price each bar — locks in profits as price rises. ATR doesn't indicate direction — only volatility magnitude.
What is algorithmic trading and how does it work?

Algorithmic (algo) trading: Computer programs execute trades based on pre-defined rules automatically. Types: Execution algorithms: Break large orders into smaller pieces to minimise market impact (VWAP, TWAP execution). Statistical arbitrage: Exploit price inefficiencies between related instruments. Market making: Continuously quote bid/ask, profit from spread. High-frequency trading (HFT): Thousands of trades per second, microsecond latency. Trend following: MA crossovers, breakout systems — run systematically. Mean reversion: Automated pairs trading. Common languages: Python (backtesting), C++ (low-latency execution). Platforms: Interactive Brokers API, Alpaca, MetaTrader. Key components: Backtesting engine, risk management module, execution layer, monitoring system. Challenges: Overfitting historical data. Market regime changes. Execution slippage. Regulatory compliance. Most retail algos use Python + broker API — HFT requires co-location and custom hardware.
What is a trading journal and why is it essential?

Trading journal: Systematic record of all trades including entry/exit, reasoning, emotions, and outcome. What to record: Date/time, instrument, direction, entry/exit price, position size, stop/target. Pre-trade thesis: Why did you take this trade? What pattern/setup? Post-trade review: What happened? Did you follow your plan? Emotional state: Were you fearful, greedy, FOMO? P&L per trade. Why it matters: Pattern recognition in your own mistakes. Identifies: Over-trading certain times of day. Poor performance on certain setups. Emotional decisions after losses (revenge trading). Discipline tracking. Improvement: Review journal weekly. Identify three recurring mistakes. Focus next week on eliminating one. Elite traders attribute journal discipline as key differentiator. Without measurement, no improvement is possible.
Explain order flow and market microstructure basics.

Order flow: The actual stream of buy and sell orders entering the market — the raw material prices are made from. Market microstructure: Study of how trades execute and prices form. Key concepts: Bid-ask spread: Difference between best buy and sell offer. Tighter in liquid markets. Market makers profit from spread. Depth of book (Level 2): Shows all pending orders at each price level. Large orders (icebergs) hide true size. Tape reading / time & sales: Real-time print of every trade — size, price, direction. Imbalances: When buy orders overwhelm sell orders (or vice versa) price moves. Tools: DOM (Depth of Market), footprint charts (volume at each price within candle), delta (difference between buying and selling volume). Institutional footprints: Large block trades, unusual options activity, dark pool prints — suggest institutional activity. Why it matters: Price is set by order flow — understanding it gives edge beyond price patterns alone.
What is the wash sale rule and how does it affect traders?

Wash sale rule (US tax law): If you sell a security at a loss and repurchase the same or 'substantially identical' security within 30 days before or after the sale — the loss is disallowed for tax purposes. 61-day window: 30 days before + sale day + 30 days after. Disallowed loss: Added to cost basis of repurchased shares (deferred, not permanently lost). Applies to: Same stock, options on same stock, substantially identical funds. Does NOT apply to: Crypto (currently — regulatory change pending). Gains — only losses affected. Strategy implications: Plan loss harvesting at year-end carefully. Wait 31 days before re-buying sold position. Replace with similar but non-identical ETF to maintain market exposure. Traders with high turnover must track wash sales meticulously — brokers may not correctly aggregate across accounts. Consult tax professional for complex situations.
How do professional traders manage drawdowns?

Drawdown: Percentage decline from portfolio peak to trough. Max drawdown: Worst peak-to-trough decline in history. Professional standards: Hedge funds typically target max drawdown <15–20%. Drawdown exceeding 20–25% triggers risk review. Rules for managing drawdowns: 1. Reduce position size immediately as drawdown increases. At −5%: cut size 25%. At −10%: cut size 50%. At −15%: stop trading, review. 2. Never add to losing positions hoping for recovery (averaging down). 3. Identify cause: Was it market conditions or strategy failure? 4. Don't try to make back losses quickly — 'revenge trading' compounds drawdowns. Mathematical reality: −50% drawdown requires +100% gain to recover. −25% requires +33%. Protect capital first — profits second. Howard Marks: 'The first rule of compounding — never interrupt it unnecessarily.'
How do you use moving averages in trading?

MOVING AVERAGES — Smoothing price data to identify trends.

SIMPLE MOVING AVERAGE (SMA):
Average of closing prices over N periods.
SMA(20) = sum of last 20 closes / 20.
As new close added, oldest dropped.

EXPONENTIAL MOVING AVERAGE (EMA):
Weighted: more recent prices get higher weight.
EMA multiplier = 2/(N+1). EMA20 multiplier = 2/21 = 0.095.
EMA today = (Close - EMA yesterday) × 0.095 + EMA yesterday.
EMA reacts faster to recent price changes than SMA.

USES:
Trend identification: price above SMA200 = generally uptrend. Below = downtrend.
Dynamic support/resistance: SMA50 often acts as support in uptrend.
 Price pulls back to SMA50, bounces -> good entry opportunity in bull market.

CROSSOVERS:
Golden cross: SMA50 crosses above SMA200. Bullish signal. Buy signal.
Death cross: SMA50 crosses below SMA200. Bearish signal. Sell signal.
EMA9 cross EMA21: shorter-term signal. Used on daily charts for swing trading.
MACD (MA Convergence Divergence): built on EMA crossovers. See indicator entry.

MA ENVELOPE:
Bands at fixed % above and below MA (e.g. MA20 ± 2.5%).
Price touching upper band = overbought. Lower band = oversold.

LIMITATIONS:
Lagging indicator: based on past prices. By time MA signals, move already happened.
Whipsaws: in sideways market, price keeps crossing MA -> false signals, losing trades.
Different parameters for different timeframes:
 Day traders: EMA9, EMA21.
 Swing traders: EMA21, SMA50.
 Investors: SMA50, SMA200.

PRACTICAL:
Trend traders: enter when price pulls back to EMA in established trend.
Use MA as trailing stop: exit when price closes below MA.
Combine with volume: MA crossover on high volume = stronger signal.
What are the most reliable chart patterns for traders?

CHART PATTERNS — Reliability and Trading Rules

REVERSAL PATTERNS (end current trend):

HEAD AND SHOULDERS (most reliable bearish reversal):
Three peaks: left shoulder, head (highest), right shoulder (similar height to left).
Neckline: connects troughs between shoulders.
Entry: break below neckline (on volume).
Target: height of head above neckline, projected down from neckline.
Failure rate: ~20%. One of most studied patterns.

DOUBLE TOP (bearish):
Price hits same high twice with moderate pullback between.
Entry: break below the pullback low (confirmation level).
Target: distance from high to confirmation level, projected down.
Triple top: three touches = stronger signal.

DOUBLE BOTTOM (bullish): mirror image.
Entry: break above the pullback high (neckline).

CONTINUATION PATTERNS (trend resumes):

FLAG (bull/bear):
Sharp move (flagpole) -> brief consolidation in opposite direction (flag) -> continuation.
Bull flag: sharp up move -> slight downward channel -> breakout up.
Entry: break above upper channel line.
Target: flagpole height added to breakout point.
Most reliable in strong trending market.

ASCENDING TRIANGLE (bullish):
Flat resistance (sellers at same price) + rising support (buyers getting more aggressive).
Buyers overcoming sellers. Entry: break above resistance on volume.

DESCENDING TRIANGLE (bearish):
Falling resistance + flat support. Bears overcoming bulls.

SYMMETRICAL TRIANGLE:
Both resistance and support converging. Neutral until breakout.
Trade in direction of breakout. Volume confirms.

CUP AND HANDLE (bullish):
Long rounded bottom (cup) + small consolidation/pullback (handle).
Entry: break above handle''s resistance (rim of cup).
Target: cup depth added to breakout.

TRADING RULES FOR PATTERNS:
Wait for confirmation: don''t enter until breakout occurs.
Volume confirms: breakout on above-average volume = stronger signal.
Failed pattern = trade the failure: H&S fails to break down -> strong bullish signal.
Multiple timeframe: pattern on weekly + confirmed on daily = stronger.
